title: Food
summary: Foodways on Native Long Island include shellfish, fish, plants, animals, planting, storage, seasonal movement, and contemporary stewardship rather than a single static diet.
content:
Introduction

From the Archaic to Late Woodland cultural periods, there has been extensive use of Long Island's maritime resources - fish, fowl, sea mammals, and shellfish - as well as small mammals, nuts, berries, tubers and extensive vegetable resources. Because of this rich food base, the gardening of domesticates here was late in time, less than 1,000 years ago (not long before the European 'discovery' of the region in the 1600s), and apparently not as extensive as elsewhere.

However, long before these domesticates were cultivated here, native women are known to have nurtured many plants - mallow, chenopodium, groundnuts (called 'sagaponack' locally), Jerusalem artichoke, etc. elsewhere and presumably here also. Evidence of the domesticated sunflower has been found in the southeast dating to over 4,000 years, and this is to the east of where domestication probably began, so there is little doubt it was also on Long Island.1

Three Sisters Plants - Corn, Bean, Squash

Maize (corn) horticulture is believed to have traveled to North America from Mesoamerica, but the squash family was Indigenous to the midwest and southeast; the corn, beans, and squash cultigens apparently reached Long Island from the midwest, perhaps through extensions of the trade networks mentioned earlier. Archaeological evidence of maize horticulture on the Island is sparse, as no known "planting fields" have been found by the first settlers in Southold, Setauket, Oyster Bay, etc.1

Winter

Seafood was smoked and dried in preparation for winter. Roots were especially important in Winter.2

Roots were especially important in Winter. Tuber roots can be harvested in the late fall and during winter thaws and were a highly valued source of carbohydrates. The plant could be left in natural storage for the winter months when other food supplies might run low. Some Shinnecock still gather Jerusalem artichokes today. 3

  1.  Gaynell Stone, Transcript of Lecture on The Material History of the Montaukett, 1998, pp. 2[↩][↩]
  2. The Indians of Long Island, An Exhibition Presented by Suffolk County Historical Society, brochure[↩]
  3. John Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700, pp 64[↩]

Foodways Across Time

Food history should connect estuaries, shellfish, fish, berries, nuts, plants, gardens, hunting, and seasonal movement. The point is not to list foods alone, but to show how people cared for and understood different habitats across the year.

Modern examples such as the Shinnecock Oyster Project help readers see foodways as continuity, stewardship, and community knowledge rather than only archaeological evidence.

Shinnecock foodways in Hunter's 1950 account

Lois Marie Hunter connected Shinnecock food knowledge with agriculture, gathering, fishing, shellfishing, and seasonal storage. She described nausaump as a corn food prepared for winter keeping, succotash made with green corn and shell beans, and knowledge of edible plants, herbs, berries, eels, clams, and other seafood. Her account also describes teaching newcomers how to plant corn and recognize productive ground. This is a historical account, not a modern recipe or foraging guide.1

Women's labor and family continuity

Shinnecock women were central to gardens, gathering, drying and storing food, cooking seafood, caring for households, and sustaining children during long whaling voyages. That labor belongs to the history of agriculture and maritime work as well as domestic life. Hunter's 1950 chapter uses dated language, but its central argument is that women's knowledge and work were indispensable to Shinnecock community survival.2

Food, work, and seasonal knowledge in the 2014 catalogue

Razor clams

The Atlantic jackknife or razor clam is described through the knowledge needed to recognize its presence in tidal ground. The entry remembers the contrast between hand gathering and later mechanized extraction.4

Places named in the catalogue

Shinnecock Bay; Great South Bay.4

Hard clams / quahogs

Hard clams connect Shinnecock meals with tools, agriculture, and wampum. The catalogue describes white and purple shell beads as meaningful objects within relationships of exchange, and distinguishes those relationships from the monetary value imposed in colonial trade.5

Places named in the catalogue

Great South Bay; Shinnecock Bay; Peconic Bay; Montauk Bay.5

Soft-shell clams / steamers

Steamers are remembered as food gathered with clam rakes from tidal areas. The catalogue also records concern in 2013 about changing estuarine conditions and the survival of formerly abundant clams.6

Places named in the catalogue

Long Island Sound; Atlantic Ocean; Shinnecock Bay; Mecox Bay; Montauk Bay; Peconic Bay; Napeague Bay; Great South Bay.6

Watercress

Elders recalled gathering watercress when they were young in the early 1900s and selling it to people in Southampton. They remembered selling it more often than eating it at home.6

Places named in the catalogue

Heady Crick.6

Geese

Geese supplied food and feathers, including fans used around fires and in clothing. Elders’ accounts of hunting at The Point emphasize care around nests and rules followed by outsiders hunting on Shinnecock land in the 1980s. The catalogue lists Canada geese, brant, and snow geese.7

Places named in the catalogue

Shinnecock territories; The Point; East End of Long Island.7

Wild grapes

Elders described gathering grapes together and spending time in one another’s kitchens making preserves and other foods. Vines were also used in basket weaving. The account makes shared work and the passing on of knowledge central to the fruit’s story.8

Places named in the catalogue

Shinnecock Hills; Shinnecock residential territories.8

Highbush and lowbush blueberries

Elders recalled berry picking on Shinnecock lands, at West Woods, and in the Pine Barrens. The catalogue describes berries dried for later use, used with meat, and added to samp with corn. Gathering and preservation extended the value of a short season.9

Places named in the catalogue

Shinnecock residential territories; West Woods; Pine Barrens; Shinnecock Hills.9

Page references

The Shinnecock Environmental Department compiled this catalogue from elders’ memories and community resource knowledge in 2014. Food and medicine appear here as historical knowledge; safe identification and treatment require current guidance.

Shinnecock Environmental Department, Natural Resources Identified by Shinnecock Elders, April 4, 2014, PDF pp. 6, 7, 12, 13, 17, 19, 20. Page numbers count the cover as PDF page 1.
